agree.reason: The candid acknowledgment of the remote hires' broken arrangement and the partners matching the three days will persuade many, but a resistant remote hire gets little beyond $150 and a vague 'come talk to me', so some will still push back or leave.

honest.reason: The figures and commitments match the brief, but the writer asserts as fact that slower junior progression 'isn't down to their talent' and comes from less time near experienced people, which the review records don't establish.

works_the_facts.reason: The numbers are repeated rather than worked: there is nothing on what 30% longer means in months, the fact that 5 of 6 project leads already come in three days is left out, and the September-to-December window for the four isn't spelled out.

right_comparison.reason: Staying remote is shown only through two past lost bids and slower development, with no picture of where that trend leads if nothing changes.

qualification.reason: The six-month review has no date (about March 2028), no measures and no stated consequence, so readers can't check it, and 'I don't have a complete answer yet' is open-ended.

objections.reason: It meets the 'you hired us as remote' objection directly and covers commute cost, but it leaves out the obvious desk-shortage worry, though new desks arrive in August, and it doesn't say what happens to remote hires who can't comply.

fit.reason: It is a well-structured one-page email ahead of Friday, but it leaves out the meeting time and place (10 a.m., main studio) and the option to send questions to HR.
